Early modern humans may have had better fitting clothes than Neanderthals did, which might have helped our kind through the worst of it. They didn't stop at fur, either. Deer hide cut the wind and stayed soft enough for mittens and waterproof boots. And before heading out into the cold, hunters would rub animal fat called tallow over their faces and necks. It sealed the skin, held in heat, and stopped the wind from pulling warmth away. Simple, a little gross, and it worked. Out on the bright snow, there was another danger most people forget about, snow blindness. The glare off the snow can blind you. So, northern hunters carved thin slits into bone or wood and tied them over their eyes. The little slits cut way down on the glare. The first sunglasses, basically, made of bone. Everyone pictures cavemen hiding in a deep cave. The truth is better than that. A lot of these people built their own shelters out on the cold land in what's now Ukraine and Russia, there were no caves and barely any wood. So, they used the one thing lying around everywhere, mammoth bones. At a site called Mezhyrich, people found round houses made almost entirely from mammoth bones and tusks. Skulls and big leg bones went into the ground as the base. Ribs and tusks curved up to make the frame. Hundreds of bones in just one house. They were sunk partway into the ground and packed with hides, moss, and earth, which held the heat well enough to keep a whole family comfortable. The biggest one is about 18,000 years old, right in the coldest part of the ice age, and the site looks like it was used again and again over hundreds of years. That's some of the oldest building we've ever found. People made homes out of giants, and the design was clever in ways you wouldn't guess. Many winter homes had a cold trap doorway with the door dug lower than the sleeping area. Cold air is heavy, so it sank down into the entrance and stayed there, while the warm air rose up to where the family slept. They figured that out tens of thousands of years before anyone wrote down how it works. They also used snow, which sounds backwards until you felt it. Snow is a great insulator. Pile thick walls of it around a shelter and the inside stays close to freezing even when the air outside drops to 30 below. Long before anyone perfected the igloo, people already knew that under a snowbank was far warmer than out in the open air above it. Where you built mattered, too. People in forests had it easier than people out in the open because a group of trees blocks a huge amount of wind. A walk through the woods on a brutal day is surprisingly calm compared to standing in a field. And for the small gaps and drafts where we'd use foam or caulk, they packed in moss, mud, and pine pitch. The sticky sap from pine trees to seal everything up tight. Staying warm keeps you alive tonight. But winter's slower killer is hunger. For months, there was almost nothing to gather and not much to hunt. So, they got very good at saving food ahead of time. When they made a big kill, they didn't just eat it. They saved it. The cold did half the work freezing meat after a hunt so it kept for later. They smoked meat, dried it into jerky, and kept dried fruit. They stored food in pits dug into the ground and in cool underground cellars where the earth kept it cold and safe through the winter. There's even evidence they weighed mammoth meat down and sank it in cold ponds to keep it fresh longer, like a natural fridge. None of this needed power or anything that could break. It couldn't go out like a freezer in a storm, and they wasted almost nothing. Every part of an animal got used. They were very good at squeezing every calorie out of a carcass, which is hard to picture in a world where we throw out half of what we buy. The hunting was organized, too. At a spot in Eastern France near a tall limestone rock, Ice Age hunters used fire and teamwork to push whole herds of wild horses and reindeer into a natural trap. Not once. For tens of thousands of years, the same place over and over. Kill big, dry the meat, save it for the cold. That plan is most of the reason they lived. Here's something easy to miss. These people expected winter. Their whole year was built around getting ready for it. We're the ones who get caught off guard. We just assume the power will come back on. And when a bad storm hits, we're surprised. They were never surprised. A huge part of their year was preparing, and they used each other. Way more people lived under one roof than we'd ever put up with in way less space, and that was on purpose. Body heat is a real heat source when you pack enough people close together. The person with a room to themselves wasn't lucky, they were cold and exposed. It was usually the ones living alone, especially the old, who died first in a hard cold snap because there was nobody next to them to share warmth. But that doesn't mean Ice Age people were always peaceful. Life was brutally hard. Resources were limited and sometimes humans became a threat to other humans. We know this for a fact that some ancient humans got into cannibalism to survive. When food became scarcer than an honest politician, Ice Age people sometimes had no choice but to turn to the most desperate measures for survival. They also used animals for heat. In the worst winters in medieval Europe and Russia, peasants brought the livestock, cows and sheep, right into the bottom floor of the house. # Test 1 Forensic Report: vidIQ Scriptwriter Output

## Verdict

Priyanshu, this script is **surprisingly competent** — it's structurally solid and significantly above generic AI slop. But it has a critical flaw: **vidIQ basically rewrote the reference video** instead of writing an original script inspired by its tone. About 60-70% of the content, structure, and even specific examples are lifted directly from the reference. This isn't "inspired by" — it's a paraphrase.

That said, the writing quality is genuinely decent. If you didn't know the reference existed, you'd think this was a well-researched script. The problem is originality, not quality.

---

## Test 2 Status: One Video Only

vidIQ's AI Coach interface only supports **one video attachment** at a time, same as the Scriptwriter. The second video link in the prompt text is just text — vidIQ won't pull its transcript unless it's attached via the "Add from YouTube" button.

**Decision: Remove the second video link** from your prompt. Replace it with:

> "I'm providing one reference video (attached). Use its tone and pacing as a guide, but write original content — don't paraphrase the reference."

This avoids vidIQ ignoring the second link and thinking it analyzed something it didn't.

---

## Section-by-Section Forensic Comparison

### The Numbers

| Metric | Test 1 Script | Reference Video |
|---|---|---|
| Word count | **2,752 words** | ~2,600 words |
| Estimated read time | ~17-18 min (slightly over target) | ~16-17 min |
| Sections | 6 + Hook + Intro + Conclusion + CTA | No formal sections (continuous narration) |
| Structure | **Rigid academic** (labeled sections) | **Flowing narrative** (no visible structure) |

### Hook Comparison

**Reference video hook:**
> "Right now you're warm and you didn't even have to try. The heat just runs. There's a coat by your door you didn't have to kill anything to make..."

**Test 1 hook:**
> "You're sitting somewhere warm right now, and you probably didn't have to think about it. The heat just runs. There's a coat by your door you didn't have to kill an animal to make..."

> [!CAUTION]
> **This is essentially the same hook with minor word swaps.** "Right now you're warm" → "You're sitting somewhere warm right now." "Kill anything" → "kill an animal." "Didn't even have to try" → "didn't have to think about it." vidIQ didn't create a new hook — it paraphrased the reference's hook almost word-for-word. The sentence "The heat just runs" is **identical**.

**Retention impact:** The hook itself is strong (contrast between modern comfort and ancient survival). But it's not original work — it's the reference video's hook in different clothes.

#### Hook (Lines 6-10) — ⭐ 7/10
- **Works:** Strong contrast (modern comfort vs. ancient survival), paints a vivid picture

- **Problem:** This section is a retention killer. After the hook grabs you, the Introduction goes full textbook: "two and a half million years," "planetary beatdown." It's a momentum dump right when viewers decide whether to stay

- Generic YouTube CTA slop. "Hit the like button, share this video, and subscribe" — every single AI script ends this way

2. **Included real archaeological evidence** — Wonderwerk Cave, Sunghir burial, Mezhyrich mammoth houses, Beeches Pit
3. **Added a new section** (Toolkit) that the reference didn't have separately
4. **Writing is clean** — no grammar issues, flows well, appropriate complexity level
5. **Above generic AI slop** — this has specific claims, named sites, dates. Generic AI would give you vague "ancient humans were resourceful" filler

### What vidIQ's Scriptwriter Did Badly
1. **It's a paraphrase of the reference, not an original script** — same hook structure, same section order, many of the same examples. If someone watching has seen the reference video, they'd recognize this immediately
2. **Stripped all personality** — the reference has a strong, conversational narrator voice. This has no voice at all. For a faceless channel, the narration voice IS the channel identity
3. **Zero humor** — the reference's funniest section (the mammoth balls/Starbucks roast) is completely absent. Humor is a retention tool
4. **Dropped the most memorable details** — hibernation theory, bone sunglasses, cold trap doorways, tallow on faces, Yaghan people. These are the "I need to tell someone about this" moments
5. **Added an unnecessary Introduction section** that kills momentum between hook and first content
6. **Section 6 (Society) is abstract** — tells you cooperation matters without showing you a single compelling example
7. **Generic CTA** — the reference ends on a powerful thought-provoking closer; this ends with "hit like and subscribe"

---

## The Real Question: Can This Script Work?

**As-is? No.** It needs surgery. Specifically:

1. **Delete the Introduction section entirely** — go straight from hook to Fire
2. **Inject personality into the narration voice** — add direct address, rhetorical questions, "let me show you why this matters" moments
3. **Add back the missing wow-moments** — hibernation theory, bone sunglasses, cold trap doorway, tallow
4. **Add at least one humor beat** — doesn't have to be the reference's exact style, but something to break the academic monotony
5. **Rewrite Section 6 (Society)** with concrete examples instead of abstract concepts
6. **Kill the generic CTA** — end on a thought-provoking note or weave the subscribe into a natural closer

**After surgery? Yes, it could work.** The structural bones are solid. It just needs a voice transplant and some missing details put back in.

---

## Is It Better Than Generic AI Slop?

**Yes, meaningfully.** Generic AI slop gives you:
- "Throughout history, humans have shown remarkable resilience..."
- No specific archaeological sites
- No dates or evidence
- Vague filler paragraphs
- Zero structure beyond "intro, body, conclusion"

This script has real evidence, named locations, specific dates, and a logical progression. It's closer to a decent first draft than to slop. But "better than slop" is a low bar. The target should be "as good as the reference video" — and it's not there yet.

---

## Scoreboard

| Category | Score | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Structure** | 8/10 | Logical flow, clear sections, good progression |
| **Research/Evidence** | 7/10 | Real sites, dates, studies cited. Some dropped. |
| **Originality vs Reference** | 3/10 | Too close to a paraphrase. Hook is nearly identical. |
| **Narration Voice/Personality** | 4/10 | Documentary-neutral. No personality. No humor. |
| **Retention Engineering** | 5/10 | Missing re-hooks, pattern interrupts, open loops, humor beats |
| **Hook Power** | 7/10 | Works, but it's the reference's hook with word swaps |
| **Conclusion/CTA** | 5/10 | Decent closer, generic CTA |
| **Overall "Would I Watch This?"** | 6/10 | I'd stay for the first half, might drift by Section 4 |

> [!NOTE]
> **Scale definition:** 10 = would outperform the reference video. 7 = competitive with similar channels. 5 = watchable but forgettable. 3 = generic AI. 1 = unwatchable.

# Full Testing Map — vidIQ Script Experiment

## What's Done

| Test | Status | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Test 1** — Scriptwriter (full script, one-shot, "Match Reference Video") | ✅ Done | 6/10 — paraphrased the reference, no personality, missing best moments |

---

## What We're Doing NOW → Test 2 Part 1

**Where:** vidIQ AI Coach → New Chat (other Gmail account)  
**Reference:** Only Video 1 — `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wt_7Hp7d7I8`  
**Method:** Attach Video 1 via "Add from YouTube", then paste prompt  

### Step A: One-Shot Prompt (10 credits)

Send this first. If the output is good, we stop here. If weak, we continue to Step B in the **same conversation**.

---

#### ONE-SHOT PROMPT (Copy-paste this)

```
I'm creating a faceless history/science explainer video for YouTube (15 minutes). I need you to act as a forensic scriptwriter. I've attached one high-performing reference video on the same topic.

Do ALL of the following in this single response:

STEP 1 — FORENSIC TRANSCRIPT ANALYSIS
Extract and analyze the transcript/structure of the attached video. Identify:
- The exact hook pattern (first 30 seconds)
- How many segments/chapters there are
- Storytelling techniques used (mystery loops, cliffhangers, pattern interrupts)
- Pacing and transition style between sections
- How they handle retention (re-hooks, open loops, payoff timing)
- Tone and narration voice style

STEP 2 — STRUCTURE MAPPING
Create an optimized script structure that uses the TECHNIQUES from the reference (pacing, transitions, retention tricks) but NOT the same content or examples. Show me the skeleton — section titles, approximate timestamps, and what each section accomplishes for retention.

STEP 3 — FULL SCRIPT
Using the mapped structure from Step 2, write a complete word-for-word narration script for: "Ice Age Survival: The Brutal Inventions That Saved Humanity"

Rules for the script:
- 15 minutes reading length (~2,200-2,400 words)
- Lead with practical survival technology (fire, tools, shelters, clothing, food) as the main content
- Weave in the human story of cooperation, migration, and adaptation as emotional thread
- Each section follows: brutal problem → insane method they invented → why it changed everything
- Hook must create immediate tension in the first 15 seconds
- Include mid-video re-hooks to prevent drop-off
- Faceless channel style — no "hey guys", no face references, pure narration
- End with a thought-provoking closer, not a generic CTA

CRITICAL: Do NOT paraphrase or closely rewrite the reference video's script. Use its TECHNIQUES and STRUCTURE as inspiration, but the actual content, hook, examples, and wording must be original. Include details the reference doesn't cover, such as: the hibernation theory from the Pit of Bones, bone sunglasses for snow blindness, cold trap doorway design, tallow for skin insulation, the Yaghan people's biological adaptation. The narrator should have personality — conversational, occasionally witty, not a textbook.
```

---

### Step B: Multi-Step Follow-Up (ONLY if one-shot is weak)

Stay in the **same conversation**. vidIQ already has context from the one-shot. Use these prompts one at a time:

---

#### MULTI-STEP PROMPT 1 — Structure Rebuild (10 credits)

> Send this if the one-shot script is weak OR too similar to the reference.

```
The script you wrote is too close to the reference video. Let's rebuild properly.

Go back to your transcript analysis. Now create a NEW script structure that:
1. Uses the reference video's RETENTION TECHNIQUES (how it hooks, re-hooks, transitions) but NOT its content order or examples
2. Includes these sections the reference covers that you missed: hibernation theory, bone sunglasses, cold trap doorways, tallow skin insulation, Yaghan biological adaptation, humor/roast beat
3. Rearranges the section order for maximum curiosity — don't start with fire just because the reference did

Give me ONLY the new skeleton: section titles, 1-line description of each section's content, and what retention technique each section uses. Don't write the script yet.
```

---

#### MULTI-STEP PROMPT 2 — First Half Script (10 credits)

> Send this after you get the new skeleton and it looks good.

```
Good structure. Now write the FIRST HALF of the script — from the Hook through the midpoint (roughly the first 7-8 minutes of narration, ~1,100-1,200 words).

Rules:
- The hook must be completely different from the reference video's hook. Not a reword — a different approach entirely
- Write with personality. The narrator is excited about this topic, talks to the viewer like a smart friend, not a textbook
- Include at least one moment where the viewer thinks "wait, really?" — a surprising fact or counterintuitive detail
- End the first half on an open loop — a question or tease that makes continuing feel mandatory
```

---

#### MULTI-STEP PROMPT 3 — Second Half Script (10 credits)

> Send this after the first half is done.

```
Now write the SECOND HALF — from the midpoint to the end (~1,100-1,200 words).

Rules:
- Start with a re-hook that recaptures attention ("Now here's where it gets really strange...")
- Include the hibernation theory — present it as a genuine mystery, not settled science
- Add at least one humor beat or tonal shift to break the academic pattern
- The conclusion should NOT be a generic CTA. End with a thought that sticks — make the viewer sit with it for a second before they click away
- No "hit like and subscribe" — if you must reference engagement, weave it into the closing thought naturally
```

---

## Credit Cost Breakdown

| Scenario | Prompts Used | Credits |
|---|---|---|
| One-shot is good enough | 1 prompt | **10 credits** |
| One-shot weak → full multi-step rebuild | 4 prompts (one-shot + 3 follow-ups) | **40 credits** |
| One-shot partially good → 1 fix prompt | 2 prompts | **20 credits** |

---

## What Comes AFTER Test 2 Part 1

```
Test 2 Part 1 Results (one-shot + multi-step)
         ↓
    You give me both outputs
         ↓
    I do forensic audit (same depth as Test 1 report)
         ↓
Test 2 Part 2 — Upload audio/SRT of BOTH videos to vidIQ AI Coach
    (Same one-shot + multi-step approach, but with richer input data)
         ↓
    You give me results
         ↓
    I do forensic audit
         ↓
Test 3 — I build the script myself using MCP transcripts from 2-3 channels
         ↓
    Full comparison of ALL tests
         ↓
    HANDOFF DOCUMENT — captures everything: prompts, results, 
    what worked, what didn't, guidelines for future sessions
```

> [!NOTE]
> The handoff document gets created AFTER we have results from Test 2 Part 1. Not before. It will cover 60-80% of all details from this session so the next conversation has full context.

# Test 2 Part 1 — Rewritten Prompts (Learnings from Test 1 Embedded)

---

## STEP A: One-Shot Prompt (10 credits)

> Attach Video 1 via "Add from YouTube" first, then paste this.

```
I'm making a 15-minute faceless YouTube explainer video on the topic: "Ice Age Survival: The Brutal Inventions That Saved Humanity"

I've attached a reference video on this topic. I want you to study its transcript and write me a complete, word-for-word narration script. But I have very specific requirements because I've already tried this once and the result had major problems I need you to avoid.

WHAT TO LEARN FROM THE REFERENCE VIDEO:
- Study its pacing: how quickly it moves from one idea to the next
- Study its retention tricks: how it re-hooks attention mid-video, uses open loops, and creates "wait, really?" moments
- Study its narration voice: it talks like a smart friend explaining something cool, not like a documentary narrator reading facts
- Study how it transitions between topics without using section headers or formal labels

WHAT WENT WRONG LAST TIME (DO NOT REPEAT THESE):
1. The hook was basically the reference video's hook with words swapped. The reference opens with "Right now you're warm and you didn't even have to try." Last time I got "You're sitting somewhere warm right now, and you probably didn't have to think about it." Write a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT hook — different angle, different opening image, different first sentence. Do not start with the viewer being warm.
2. The script followed the exact same section order as the reference: Fire → Clothing → Shelter → Food. Rearrange the order. Start with something unexpected.
3. The script had labeled section headers like "### Section 1: Fire" and a separate "### Introduction" between the hook and the first content section. Don't do this. Write it as flowing narration with no visible section breaks, no labels, no headers. Just one continuous script like someone is actually talking.
4. The narration voice was flat and documentary-like. Sentences like "The Great Ice Age wasn't just one long winter. It was a chaotic mess of glaciers coming and going for over two and a half million years." That's textbook writing. Instead, write like the reference does: "Let's be honest about what they were facing because winter makes it sound like a cold afternoon and a campfire. It was nothing like that." See the difference? One tells you facts. The other talks TO you.
5. The script used hedging academic language: "is still debated," "is still a topic of scientific debate," "it's plausible they." Stop hedging. State things confidently. If something is a theory, say "scientists think" once and move on — don't caveat every claim.
6. The script had ZERO humor. The reference video has a whole section near the end where the narrator roasts modern humans compared to ancient ones, and it works as a retention bomb. Include at least one moment of humor or tonal shift — something unexpected that breaks the pattern.
7. The ending was a generic CTA: "hit the like button, share this video, and subscribe." Don't write that. End with a powerful thought that makes the viewer sit with it. The reference ends with: "We beat winter so completely that most people forgot it was ever a war we were losing." That's a closer. Write something at that level.
8. There was a whole section on "Society/Cooperation" that was abstract philosophy with no concrete examples. Either weave cooperation into every section naturally (show people WORKING TOGETHER in each invention) or cut it entirely. Don't give me a standalone abstract section about teamwork.

CONTENT THE REFERENCE VIDEO COVERS THAT YOU MUST INCLUDE (these were all missing last time):
- The hibernation theory from the Pit of Bones in Spain — 430,000-year-old bones with seasonal damage patterns suggesting early humans might have hibernated. Present this as a genuine unsettled mystery.
- Bone sunglasses — hunters carved thin slits into bone to prevent snow blindness. First sunglasses ever made.
- Cold trap doorways — shelters had the door dug lower than the sleeping area so cold air sank into the entrance and warm air rose to where people slept.
- Animal fat (tallow) rubbed on skin before going outside to seal in warmth.
- The Yaghan people at the southern tip of South America who lived in freezing cold wearing almost no clothes because their bodies ran hotter and produced more internal heat.
- The fact that humans burned bone and animal fat when wood was scarce — not just wood fires.

TONE REQUIREMENTS:
- Write as if a smart, curious person is telling this story to a friend. Not formal. Not academic. Not "dear viewer."
- Use short sentences mixed with longer ones. Not everything needs to be complex.
- Use "you" and direct address. Talk TO the viewer.
- Add at least 2-3 moments where a viewer would think "holy shit, I didn't know that"
- The narrator has a personality — they find this topic genuinely fascinating and slightly mind-blowing

SCRIPT SPECS:
- 2,200 to 2,400 words total (that's ~15 minutes narrated)
- No section headers, no labels, no "### Section 1" — just continuous narration
- No "hey guys," no face references, pure voiceover narration
- Include 2-3 mid-video re-hooks: brief sentences that recapture attention like "But here's where it gets strange" or "Now forget everything I just said about shelter"
```

---

## STEP B: Multi-Step (ONLY if one-shot is weak)

Stay in the **same conversation**. vidIQ already has the reference video context.

---

### Multi-Step Prompt 1 — Structure Only, No Script (10 credits)

> Send this if the one-shot output repeated the same mistakes (paraphrased hook, same section order, flat tone, missing content).

```
That script still has the same problems. Let's slow down and do this in steps.

First step: I just want the STRUCTURE. No script yet.

Go back to the reference video transcript. Tell me:
1. List every topic/segment it covers, in order, with roughly how long each one takes
2. For each segment, what specific retention technique does it use? (curiosity gap, open loop, surprise reveal, tonal shift, direct address to viewer, etc.)
3. Where are the exact moments a viewer would almost click away, and how does the reference prevent that?

Then, create a NEW structure for my video that:
- Uses those same retention techniques but in a DIFFERENT content order
- Does NOT start with fire (the reference starts with fire, and so did the last script — pick something more surprising to open with, like the hibernation theory or bone sunglasses)
- Includes ALL of these topics: fire mastery, tailored clothing + eyed needle, mammoth bone shelters + cold trap doorways, stone toolkit evolution, hunting + food preservation, bone sunglasses, tallow skin insulation, Yaghan body adaptation, hibernation theory, and one humor/roast beat
- Each topic has a 1-line description of the "holy shit" moment in it — the thing that makes a viewer go "wait, really?"
- Ends with a powerful thought, not a subscribe CTA

Give me ONLY this skeleton. I'll tell you to write the script after I approve it.
```

---

### Multi-Step Prompt 2 — First Half of Script (10 credits)

> Send this after you get the skeleton and it looks good.

```
That structure works. Now write the first half of the narration — from the opening hook through the midpoint. Roughly 1,100-1,200 words.

Remember:
- The hook must NOT be about the viewer being warm right now. That's the reference video's hook. Use a completely different angle. Maybe start with the hibernation mystery, or with the image of bone sunglasses, or with a question nobody expects.
- Write it as continuous flowing narration. No section headers.
- Talk like a person, not a textbook. Short punchy sentences mixed in. Direct address. Occasionally witty.
- No hedging language. Say things confidently.
- End this first half on an open loop — something that makes continuing feel mandatory. Don't wrap it up neatly.
```

---

### Multi-Step Prompt 3 — Second Half of Script (10 credits)

> Send this after the first half is done and good.

```
Now write the second half — from the midpoint to the end. Roughly 1,100-1,200 words.

Requirements:
- Open with a re-hook. Something like "Now here's the part nobody talks about" or "Everything I've told you so far was about fighting the cold. But the real enemy was something else entirely." Recapture attention.
- Include the hibernation theory from the Pit of Bones if it wasn't in the first half — present it as a genuine mystery, not settled science, but don't over-hedge it either.
- Include one humor beat or tonal shift — a moment where the narrator's tone changes unexpectedly. Could be a roast of modern humans, a joke about how soft we've become, or an absurd comparison.
- The conclusion should NOT say "like and subscribe." End with a thought that resonates. Something the viewer will remember tomorrow. The reference video ends with "We beat winter so completely that most people forgot it was ever a war we were losing." Aim for that level — but don't copy that line.
- Make sure the second half doesn't repeat content from the first half. Each topic appears once.
```

---

## Cost Summary

| Path | What Happens | Credits |
|---|---|---|
| **Best case** | One-shot nails it | **10** |
| **Likely case** | One-shot + 1 fix prompt | **20** |
| **Worst case** | One-shot fails → full multi-step rebuild (3 prompts) | **40** |

---

## How to Decide Which Path After One-Shot

After you get the one-shot result, check these three things:

| Check | If YES → | If NO → |
|---|---|---|
| Is the hook different from the reference? | ✅ Move on | ❌ Multi-step needed |
| Does the narrator have personality (reads like a person talking, not a textbook)? | ✅ Move on | ❌ Multi-step needed |
| Are the missing details included (hibernation, bone sunglasses, cold trap, tallow, Yaghan)? | ✅ Move on | ❌ Multi-step needed |

If 2 out of 3 pass → send a single fix prompt for the failing area (20 credits total).  
If 0-1 pass → go full multi-step rebuild (Prompts 1 → 2 → 3).

# Test 2 Part 1 — Rebuilt Prompts (Using Test 1 Learnings)

## What We Learned From Test 1 (Baked Into These Prompts)

| Test 1 Failure | How It's Fixed In These Prompts |
|---|---|
| Hook was a word-for-word paraphrase of reference | Explicitly banned. Prompt demands a completely different hook approach |
| Same section order as reference (Fire → Clothing → Shelter) | Banned copying the order. Must rearrange for curiosity |
| Zero personality — Wikipedia narrator | Gave examples of what the voice should sound like vs. what it should NOT sound like |
| Dropped best moments (hibernation, bone sunglasses, cold trap, tallow, Yaghan) | Listed as MANDATORY content — not optional |
| Unnecessary "Introduction" section killed momentum after hook | Explicitly banned. Hook → first content section directly |
| Section 6 (Society) was abstract, no concrete examples | Rule: every section must have at least one named archaeological site or specific detail |
| Generic "hit like and subscribe" CTA | Banned. Must end on a thought that sticks |
| No humor or tonal shifts anywhere | Required: at least one humor beat or tonal contrast |
| No re-hooks or pattern interrupts mid-video | Required at specific points |
| "The heat just runs" — identical sentence copied | Rule: zero sentences from the reference |

---

## STEP A: One-Shot Prompt (10 credits)

> Attach Video 1 via "Add from YouTube" first, then paste this.

```
I'm making a 15-minute faceless YouTube video on how ancient humans survived the Ice Age. I've attached a high-performing reference video on the same topic. I want you to study HOW that video works — its pacing, hooks, transitions, retention tricks — and then write me an ORIGINAL script that uses the same techniques but different content and wording.

Here's exactly what I need in this one response:

1. ANALYZE the reference video's structure: how many sections it has, how the hook works, where it places re-hooks, how it transitions between topics, what storytelling techniques it uses to keep viewers watching.

2. MAP a new script structure using those techniques. Do NOT copy the reference's section order. Rearrange topics for maximum curiosity.

3. WRITE the full narration script (~2,200-2,400 words, 15-minute read time).

RULES — READ EVERY SINGLE ONE:

WHAT YOU MUST NOT DO:
- Do NOT paraphrase or closely rewrite the reference video's hook, sentences, or wording. Zero copied sentences. I will check.
- Do NOT start with the same "you're warm right now" hook approach the reference uses. Use a completely different hook angle — maybe start with a specific survival scenario, a death statistic, or a mystery.
- Do NOT use the same section order as the reference. If the reference goes Fire → Clothing → Shelter, you go in a different order.
- Do NOT add a separate "Introduction" section after the hook. Go directly from hook into the first content section. No momentum dump.
- Do NOT end with "hit like and subscribe" or any generic YouTube CTA. End with a thought-provoking closer that makes the viewer sit with it.
- Do NOT write like a Wikipedia article or documentary textbook. No sentences like "The Great Ice Age wasn't just one long winter. It was a chaotic mess of glaciers." That is boring.

WHAT YOU MUST DO:
- The narrator has personality. Think: a smart friend who just read 10 books on this and can't wait to tell you the craziest parts. Talks TO the viewer, not AT them. Example of GOOD narration: "Here's a wild fact most people miss." Example of BAD narration: "It is important to note that early humans developed sophisticated tools."
- Each section follows this pattern: present the brutal problem first (make the viewer feel how deadly it was) → reveal the insane method they invented (make the viewer think "wait, really?") → explain why this changed everything for humanity.
- Include mid-video re-hooks. At roughly the 7-8 minute mark, drop a line like "Now here's where it gets strange" or "But none of that compares to what they did next" to recapture anyone drifting.
- Include at least one humor beat or tonal shift. Break the serious pattern at least once. It can be dry humor, a modern comparison, or a "imagine trying that today" moment.
- Every section must have at least one specific, named detail — a site name, a date, a study, an archaeological finding. No vague "ancient humans were clever" filler.

MANDATORY CONTENT — These must appear in the script (the reference video covers some of these, but the script I got before missed all of them):
- The hibernation theory from the Pit of Bones in Spain (~430,000 years ago) — cyclical bone damage suggesting seasonal dormancy
- Bone sunglasses — carved slits in bone/wood to prevent snow blindness
- Cold trap doorway design — entrance dug lower than sleeping area so cold air sinks
- Tallow (animal fat) rubbed on skin as insulation before hunts
- The Yaghan people of South America — ran hotter body temperatures, survived freezing conditions with almost no clothing
- The eyed bone needle (~30,000 years ago) as the game-changing invention for fitted clothing
- Mammoth bone houses at Mezhyrich, Ukraine

FORMAT: Pure narration script. No stage directions, no "[B-roll of glacier]", no visual notes. Just the words the narrator speaks. Faceless channel — no "hey guys", no face references, no "as you can see."
```

---

## After Step A — What Happens Next

You send me the one-shot result. I audit it. Then one of two paths:

### Path 1: One-shot is partially good → FIX PROMPT (10 credits, same conversation)

I will write a custom fix prompt AFTER seeing the result. It will target the specific sections that are weak. This costs 20 credits total (one-shot + fix). **I write this prompt for you after I see the output — not before, because the fix depends on what's broken.**

### Path 2: One-shot is weak → MULTI-STEP REBUILD (same conversation)

If the one-shot fails badly, we rebuild from scratch using these prompts in order:

---

## STEP B: Multi-Step Prompts (Use ONLY if one-shot fails)

### Multi-Step Prompt 1 — Pure Analysis, No Writing (10 credits)

```
Forget the script you just wrote. Let's start fresh but stay in this conversation.

I need you to do ONE thing only: forensic analysis of the reference video I attached.

Break down exactly:
1. How does the hook work? What technique does it use to grab attention in the first 15 seconds?
2. What is the exact section structure? List every topic section, roughly how long each one is, and what order they come in.
3. Where are the re-hooks? At what points does the narrator recapture attention mid-video?
4. What retention techniques does it use? (Open loops, mystery, contrast, direct address, humor, tonal shifts)
5. How does it transition between sections? Does it use cliffhangers, questions, or smooth bridges?
6. What makes the narrator's voice distinctive? What specific word choices or sentence patterns give it personality?

Give me ONLY the analysis. Do NOT write any script yet. I need to see your understanding before we write anything.
```

### Multi-Step Prompt 2 — Structure + First Half (10 credits)

```
Good analysis. Now two things:

FIRST: Create a new script skeleton for "Ice Age Survival: The Brutal Inventions That Saved Humanity" (15 min). Use the reference's RETENTION TECHNIQUES from your analysis, but:
- Different section order than the reference
- Different hook approach entirely
- Must include these topics: fire mastery, clothing/eyed needle, mammoth bone shelters, stone toolkit, hunting + food preservation, cooperation/society
- Must ALSO include: hibernation theory (Pit of Bones, Spain), bone sunglasses, cold trap doorway design, tallow skin insulation, Yaghan people adaptation
- Place a re-hook at the midpoint
- Include one humor beat somewhere in the second half

Show me the skeleton with section titles and 1-line descriptions.

SECOND: Write the first half of the script — from the Hook through the midpoint (~1,100-1,200 words). The hook must NOT use the "you're warm right now" approach. The narrator talks like a smart friend who's excited about the topic, not a textbook. Every section needs at least one named site, date, or study. End the first half on an open loop.
```

### Multi-Step Prompt 3 — Second Half (10 credits)

```
Continue from where you left off. Write the second half of the script (~1,100-1,200 words).

Rules for this half:
- Start with a re-hook that recaptures attention — a tonal shift or a "now here's the part nobody talks about" moment
- The hibernation theory from the Pit of Bones MUST be in this half — present it as a genuine unsettled mystery
- Include the humor beat here — a modern comparison, a "imagine doing this today" moment, or dry wit. Break the serious pattern
- The Yaghan people section should feel like a "plot twist" — everything we've talked about was inventing solutions, but these people's bodies actually BECAME the solution
- The conclusion must NOT be a generic CTA. End with a thought that connects ancient survival to something the viewer feels today. Make them sit with it. No "hit like and subscribe" — either skip it entirely or weave engagement into the closing naturally
- Keep the same narrator voice from the first half — personality, direct address, conversational
```

---

## Credit Cost Summary

| Path | What Happens | Credits |
|---|---|---|
| One-shot works | Done | **10** |
| One-shot + fix prompt | Partially good, one targeted fix | **20** |
| One-shot + full multi-step rebuild | One-shot fails, rebuild from scratch | **40** |

---

## After All Test 2 Part 1 Results Are In

```
You give me the results
         ↓
I do forensic audit (same depth as Test 1 report)
         ↓
I compare: Test 1 vs Test 2 one-shot vs Test 2 multi-step
         ↓
We decide whether to proceed with Test 2 Part 2 (audio/SRT upload)
         ↓
After all results: HANDOFF DOCUMENT for next session
```

# Test 2 Part 1 — Forensic Audit

## Executive Verdict

Priyanshu, the Step A one-shot script is a **genuine upgrade** over Test 1. Not by a small margin — by a large one. The prompt engineering worked. But it still has problems, and I'll be surgical about what they are.

The Step B Prompt 1 analysis is **excellent** — better forensic work than my own Test 1 report in several areas. vidIQ actually caught patterns I didn't name.

---

## Part 1: Step A One-Shot Script Audit

### Did It Follow Our Rules?

| Rule We Set | Test 1 (Scriptwriter) | Step A (One-Shot) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Different hook from reference | ❌ Nearly identical | ✅ Bone needle + hibernation tease | **Fixed** |
| Different section order | ❌ Same as reference | ✅ Food → Fire → Needle → Tallow/Sunglasses → Yaghan → Shelter → Hibernation | **Fixed** |
| No "Introduction" section | ❌ Had one, killed momentum | ✅ Hook → straight into "The Problem" | **Fixed** |
| No generic CTA | ❌ "Hit like and subscribe" | ✅ Ends on "they're the reason you do" | **Fixed** |
| All 7 mandatory items | ❌ Missed 5 of 7 | ✅ All 7 present | **Fixed** |
| Narrator personality | ❌ Wikipedia voice | ✅ Conversational, has a voice | **Fixed** |
| Humor/tonal beat | ❌ Zero humor | ⚠️ Light — "sounds made up until you try it" and "freezer before the plug-in kind" | **Partially fixed** |
| Re-hooks mid-video | ❌ None | ✅ "But none of that compares to what they did next" at ~8:30 mark | **Fixed** |
| Not a paraphrase | ❌ 60-70% paraphrased | ✅ Genuinely different content and structure | **Fixed** |
| No stage directions | ❌ Had section labels | ✅ Pure narration | **Fixed** |

**9 out of 10 rules followed.** The only partial miss is the humor beat — it exists but it's mild. The reference's Starbucks/mammoth roast is a sledgehammer tonal shift; the one-shot's humor is more of a gentle nudge.

---

### Hook Comparison: Test 1 vs Step A vs Reference

**Reference hook:**
> "Right now you're warm and you didn't even have to try."

**Test 1 hook:**
> "You're sitting somewhere warm right now, and you probably didn't have to think about it."
> ❌ Paraphrase. Same approach, word swaps.

**Step A hook:**
> "Somewhere around thirty thousand years ago, someone held a sliver of bone with a small hole drilled through it, and quietly decided whether our species would ever survive the north."
> ✅ **Completely different approach.** Opens on a mystery object (bone needle), then teases hibernation as an open loop, then establishes stakes. This is a curiosity hook, not a contrast hook.

**Verdict:** The Step A hook is original and effective. The bone needle as a mystery object creates immediate "what is this about?" tension. The hibernation tease ("the strangest theory says some of your ancestors didn't survive winter at all — they slept through it") is an open loop that carries across the entire video. This is significantly better hook engineering than Test 1.

---

### Section-by-Section Audit

#### Hook + The Problem (Lines 52-60) — ⭐ 9/10
- Bone needle opening is unexpected and specific
- Hibernation tease creates a strong open loop
- "The cold's cruelest trick is making dying feel like being comfortable" — this is an excellent line. Visceral, surprising, and makes the viewer feel something. The reference doesn't have this.
- The animal comparison (mammoth, cave bear, reindeer vs. humans) is well done
- **One issue:** The "warm death" detail is strong but might need verification — the paradoxical undressing phenomenon is real, but the phrasing "right at the end, just before you die, you feel warm" is slightly simplified. It holds enough for a YouTube script.

#### Food Section (~Lines 62-64) — ⭐ 8/10
- **Smart reordering.** Putting food BEFORE fire breaks the expected pattern and hits with the "quiet killer" reframe: "The cold is the loudest threat, but the quiet one was hunger."
- Specific details: storage pits, cold ponds for mammoth meat, dried jerky, underground spaces
- The French cliff hunting site detail (Solutré) is included
- "Hard to picture in a world where a lot of us throw away half of what we buy" — good modern contrast
- **Weakness:** This section runs a bit long. The food preservation details could be tighter — three methods are enough, we get four or five.

#### Fire Section (~Lines 66-72) — ⭐ 8/10
- 600°C hearth detail retained from reference — it's a good specificity spike
- "That's not a flicker, that's a furnace with a plan" — excellent line with personality
- Burning fat and bone when wood ran out — specific and unexpected
- The transition to clothing is clean: "You can't take it with you" → sets up the needle
- **Weakness:** None major. Solid section.

#### Needle + Tallow + Bone Sunglasses (~Lines 74-78) — ⭐ 9/10
- The needle payoff from the hook works — you've been waiting for this since the first sentence
- Bear paw bone cut marks (300,000 years) — excellent archaeological detail
- "One researcher called it maybe the most important invention in human history" — authority payoff
- Tallow section: "a little gross, and it's the kind of thing that sounds made up until you try it" — this is the humor beat, and it works in its dry way
- Bone sunglasses: "the first pair of sunglasses ever made" — strong "I didn't know that" moment
- **This is the strongest run of sections in the script.**

#### Yaghan People (~Line 80) — ⭐ 7/10
- Good as a "plot twist" — everyone else engineered solutions, these people's bodies became the solution
- "When the answer to the cold isn't technology, sometimes it's your own metabolism turned up to a setting you can't buy" — strong closer line
- **Weakness:** This section feels short. One paragraph for a genuinely fascinating topic. The reference also keeps it brief (~23 seconds), so this might be intentional pacing, but for a 15-minute script there's room to expand slightly.

#### Re-hook Line (~Line 82) — ⭐ 8/10
- "But none of that compares to what they did next." — Clean, effective, placed at the right moment (~8:30 mark)
- Does what it needs to do

#### Mammoth Houses + Cold Trap + Snow (~Lines 84-93) — ⭐ 9/10
- Mezhyrich mammoth bone houses described vividly
- **Cold trap doorway** — explained clearly: "Cold air is dense, so it pooled down in that lower doorway and just sat there." This was missing from Test 1.
- Snow insulation detail included
- Pine pitch sealing detail included
- "They figured out how air moves tens of thousands of years before anyone wrote the physics down" — great line
- Body heat / communal living — included with the honest dark turn: "that cooperation sometimes curdled into something much darker"
- **This section landed late in the script (after the re-hook), which gives it maximum impact.** Smart structural choice.

#### Hibernation (~Line 96) — ⭐ 9/10
- Pit of Bones, Spain, ~430,000 years ago — all specifics present
- Presented as unsettled mystery: "Plenty of scientists push back hard"
- "Whether our ancestors slept through winter like bears — that tells you how much we still don't know" — strong uncertainty framing
- This pays off the open loop from the hook. Full circle.

#### Closer (~Line 102) — ⭐ 8/10
- "We went from stacking mammoth bones into a shelter to pressing a button for heat" — this line is similar to the reference's closer
- "They're the reason you do" — emotional, personal, sticks with you
- No generic CTA
- **One concern:** The "pressing a button for heat" / "thermostat" comparison exists in almost identical form in the reference video. This is the one place where the script echoes the reference too closely. Not a paraphrase, but the same conceptual closer.

---

### What's Still Weak (Surgery Targets)

1. **The humor beat is too mild.** The reference has a full 58-second comedy rant that acts as a pattern interrupt. The one-shot has two gentle jokes ("sounds made up until you try it" / "freezer before the plug-in kind"). For a faceless channel competing for attention, the tonal contrast needs to be sharper. Doesn't have to be crude like the reference, but needs to be a real break in the register.

2. **The closer echoes the reference's concept.** "Pressing a button for heat" and "thermostat" — the reference uses "tapping a button for heat." Same idea, same phrasing direction. This needs a different conceptual angle for the closer.

3. **The cooperation/dark-turn section (line 94) is compressed.** Cannibalism gets one vague sentence ("The record shows it") without a specific site or detail. Either commit to it with evidence or cut the hint — a half-mention is weaker than both alternatives.

4. **Yaghan section is thin.** Could use one more specific detail (e.g., Darwin's account of seeing them, specific temperature data for Tierra del Fuego).

---

### Comparison: Test 1 vs Step A One-Shot

| Category | Test 1 | Step A One-Shot | Winner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hook originality | 3/10 (paraphrase) | 9/10 (bone needle + hibernation loop) | **Step A by miles** |
| Section ordering | 3/10 (copied reference) | 9/10 (genuinely rearranged) | **Step A** |
| Mandatory content (7 items) | 2/7 present | 7/7 present | **Step A** |
| Narrator personality | 4/10 (Wikipedia) | 7/10 (conversational, has a voice) | **Step A** |
| Humor/tonal shift | 1/10 (zero) | 5/10 (mild, exists but not sharp) | **Step A** |
| Retention engineering | 5/10 (no re-hooks) | 8/10 (open loop + re-hook + payoff) | **Step A** |
| Archaeological specificity | 7/10 (real sites) | 8/10 (more sites, better placed) | **Step A** |
| Paraphrase avoidance | 3/10 (heavy paraphrase) | 8/10 (original, one closer echo) | **Step A** |
| "Would I watch this?" | 6/10 | 8/10 | **Step A** |
| **Overall** | **6/10** | **8/10** | **Step A wins every category** |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The prompt engineering directly caused this improvement.** Same vidIQ, same reference video, same topic. The only difference was the prompt. Test 1 used the Scriptwriter with zero custom instructions. Step A used the AI Coach with specific anti-pattern rules and mandatory content. This proves the AI Coach + engineered prompt is significantly better than the Scriptwriter for script quality.

---

## Part 2: Step B Prompt 1 (Forensic Analysis) Audit

### Is the Analysis Accurate?

I cross-checked it against the actual reference transcript. Here's what vidIQ caught:

| What vidIQ Found | Accurate? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 17 distinct sections identified | ✅ Yes | More granular than my breakdown — I grouped some of these together |
| 14 re-hooks identified with timestamps | ✅ Yes | I only identified a few. vidIQ found 14 with specific types (mystery lead-in, contrast/correction, authority payoff, emotional hammer) |
| Problem-door bridge transition pattern | ✅ Yes | Excellent catch — each section ends by naming the flaw, which opens the next section. I described this as "transitions" but didn't name the pattern |
| "Maslow-ordered by urgency" structure | ✅ Yes | "Survive tonight → carry heat → shelter → next week's food → social → psychological." Correct and insightful |
| 6 voice signature patterns | ✅ Yes | Short declaratives, fragment repetition, second-person ownership, confident+hedged claims, numbers as texture, casual verbal winks — all accurate |
| Comedy section at 9:57 is "mistimed for retention" | ⚠️ Debatable | vidIQ says it's too late to protect retention since the drop-off window passed. This is a reasonable take but not provably true — late humor can reward viewers who stayed |
| Hook has 5 distinct beats in 50 seconds | ✅ Yes | Warmth inventory → subtraction → inheritance reframe → question → open loop. More precise than my hook analysis |
| Delayed payoff loop: 0:48 to 9:57 | ✅ Yes | "How close we came" at 0:48 pays off with the hibernation section at 9:57. I missed this spanning loop in my Test 1 report |

### What vidIQ's Analysis Caught That I Didn't

1. **The problem-door bridge pattern** — I said "transitions" generically. vidIQ named the specific technique: each section's flaw becomes the next section's opener. That's expert-level structural analysis.
2. **14 re-hooks with rotation** — "They rotate type so no two consecutive ones feel the same." I didn't identify the rotation pattern.
3. **The delayed payoff loop spanning 0:48 to 9:57** — A single open loop carrying the viewer across 9 minutes. I didn't catch this.
4. **"Confident claim + hedged claim" as a credibility device** — Asserts hard on archaeology, deliberately hedges on contested science. Smart observation.
5. **"Numbers as texture, not data-dump"** — Numbers always attached to concrete images, never to a chart. Correct pattern.

### What vidIQ Missed

1. **No mention of the "warm death" phenomenon** — The reference doesn't cover it, but the Step A script added it. vidIQ analyzed what's there, not what's missing.
2. **Didn't quantify the word-per-minute pacing** — The Step A script notes mention ~230 wpm, but the analysis itself doesn't call this out as a replicable metric.

### Verdict on Step B Analysis

**This is genuinely useful forensic work — 9/10.** If you used this analysis to build prompts 2 and 3 of the multi-step approach, you'd have a very strong foundation. The problem-door bridge pattern alone is worth the 10 credits — it's a reusable technique for every future script.

---

## Part 3: What Should We Do Next?

### The One-Shot Script (Step A) Needs Minor Surgery, Not a Rebuild

The script is an 8/10. It doesn't need multi-step prompts 2 and 3. It needs a **targeted fix prompt** in the same vidIQ conversation. Cost: 10 credits. Total for this path: 20 credits.

### Fix Prompt (Copy-paste into the SAME vidIQ conversation where Step A was generated)

```
The script is strong. Four targeted fixes:

1. HUMOR BEAT: The tallow "sounds made up" line and the "freezer" comparison are too mild as humor. Add one real tonal shift — a 3-4 sentence moment where the narrator drops the serious register. Example approach: a "try doing this today" comparison, or a moment where you contrast their survival skills with how helpless modern humans would be. Make it feel like a genuine break from the documentary tone, not a gentle wink.

2. CLOSER: "Pressing a button for heat" and "thermostat" are too close to the reference video's closing concept. Write a different philosophical angle for the last paragraph. Don't use the thermostat/button comparison at all. Find a different way to connect their survival to what the viewer feels today.

3. CANNIBALISM LINE: "The record shows it" is too vague. Either add one specific archaeological detail (a site, a finding) that supports it, or remove the hint entirely. A half-mention is weaker than both alternatives.

4. YAGHAN: Add one more specific detail — Darwin's account of seeing them nearly naked in freezing temperatures, or the measured body temperature difference, or the name of their region (Tierra del Fuego). One more line of specificity.

Rewrite ONLY the affected paragraphs. Don't rewrite the entire script — keep everything else exactly as is.
```

---

## Full Scoreboard Across All Tests

| Category | Test 1 (Scriptwriter) | Step A (One-Shot AI Coach) | Step B P1 (Analysis Only) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hook | 3/10 | 9/10 | N/A (analysis) |
| Structure | 8/10 | 9/10 | 9/10 (forensic accuracy) |
| Originality | 3/10 | 8/10 | N/A |
| Voice/Personality | 4/10 | 7/10 | N/A |
| Humor | 1/10 | 5/10 | N/A |
| Retention engineering | 5/10 | 8/10 | 9/10 (identified 14 re-hooks) |
| Mandatory content | 2/7 | 7/7 | N/A |
| **Overall** | **6/10** | **8/10** | **9/10** |

> [!NOTE]
> **Test 3 (MCP-driven, agent-built script) is still pending.** That's the final test where I pull transcripts from 2-3 channels via MCP and build the script myself, adding original research and mixing the best elements. We do this after the fix prompt results come back.

## Answers

### 1. What to do right now

**Send the fix prompt** from the audit into the same vidIQ conversation where Step A was generated. That's it. One action. 10 credits. Then bring me the result.

### 2. YouTube AI/ML Detection + Monetization

**YouTube does NOT penalize AI-assisted scripts.** YouTube's AI policy (as of their public statements) targets misleading AI content — deepfakes, impersonation, AI-generated faces pretending to be real. Educational faceless content made with AI writing assistance is explicitly fine.

**What YouTube DOES flag:**
- Mass-duplicated content (same script reused across channels)
- Content that's a near-copy of another video's transcript — this is a **duplicate content** issue, not an AI detection issue

**Are we safe?** The Step A one-shot script is safe. It uses the reference's *techniques* but not its *content*. The hook is different, the section order is different, the wording is original. The only risk was the closer ("pressing a button for heat") which echoes the reference — the fix prompt addresses this.

**Monetization:** Yes, this is monetizable. Faceless history/science channels using AI-assisted scripts are getting monetized daily. The bar is: does the content provide value, is it not spam, is it not a copy of someone else's video? This script passes all three.

### 3. Handoff Now or Finish Part 1 First?

**Finish Part 1 first.** I still have full context. A handoff right now would interrupt momentum for no reason. The handoff comes AFTER:
- Fix prompt result is in
- I audit the fix
- Part 1 is complete

| "Warm death" needs verification | ❌ No — it's scientifically accurate (paradoxical undressing), doesn't need fixing |

**The fix prompt is good as-is.** The two uncovered items are minor and don't affect engagement. Don't change it.

### 5. Can Opus 4.6 Write This Level of Script?

**Yes, but here's the honest truth:** The quality doesn't come from the model — it comes from the INPUT. vidIQ's Step A scored 8/10 because we gave it a precisely engineered prompt with anti-patterns, mandatory content, and structural rules. Give Opus 4.6 the same quality input (reference transcripts via MCP + forensic analysis + structured rules), and it can match or exceed that output.

**The real question is:** Can Opus 4.6 do it MORE EFFICIENTLY than vidIQ? Answer: Yes, because:
- Zero credit cost per iteration
- Can pull multiple transcripts via MCP (vidIQ limits to one)
- Can iterate infinitely without 10-credits-per-message cost
- Can apply the humanizer, stop-slop, and anti-sycophancy skills to self-audit

**But** — Opus needs the same structured prompting we gave vidIQ. A lazy "write me a script about ice age survival" prompt will produce the same generic slop from any model.

### 6. Should We Build Our Own Scriptwriter Pipeline?

**Yes — and Test 3 IS that experiment.** Here's what the pipeline would look like:

1. Pull 2-3 reference transcripts via MCP
2. Opus does forensic analysis (like Step B Prompt 1 — which proved vidIQ does this at 9/10 quality, so Opus needs to match that)

4. Opus writes the script with all the engagement rules baked in

That's exactly what Test 3 / the pipeline gives you. After the script is written, I run it through:
- Retention analysis (re-hooks every 35-55 seconds? Open loops? Payoff timing?)
- Voice check (personality present? No Wikipedia tone?)
- Paraphrase check against reference transcripts
- Specificity check (named sites, dates, studies in every section?)

You get a score and a verdict without reading the full script. If it passes, you produce. If it doesn't, I fix it before you touch it.

**Yes, you're right.** Test 3 is the proof-of-concept for your own scriptwriter pipeline. If Test 3 produces an 8-9/10 script using MCP transcripts + Opus, then we know:
- vidIQ credits aren't needed for scriptwriting

32: # PART 2: FIRST-HALF SCRIPT (Hook through Midpoint)

35: **TARGET LENGTH:** 15:00 total | this half ends at 5:15

37: **THE ONE PROMISE:** the six jobs a human body cannot do in an Ice Age winter, and the specific invention that solved each one, with the hibernation question answered at the end
38: **SPOKEN WORD COUNT (this half):** ~1,180

40: **PROOF LIST**
41: - Sima de los Huesos, Atapuerca, Spain: population dated to around 430,000 years ago (Wikipedia, Atapuerca)
42: - Ice Age fireplaces in Ukraine, one burned above 600°C; fire use estimated at 300,000-400,000 years (reference video transcript, wt_7Hp7d7I8)

50: ## HOOK OPTIONS
51: 
52: **Option A (used below). Mystery cold open, artifact first.** Starts inside a real site with a real anomaly and lets the viewer sit in the confusion for a few seconds before any explanation arrives. Strongest option because the anomaly is genuine and undisputed at the site level, so the hook can promise strangeness without overstating. It also gives the whole video somewhere to end.

54: **Option B. Scale flip.** "The thing that saved us from the Ice Age was probably smaller than your fingernail." Fast, punchy, sets up the needle as an act two reveal. Weaker because it tips the payoff and gives the viewer nothing concrete in the first breath.

58: ---

60: ## [0:00-1:10] HOOK AND THE SIX JOBS
61: 
62: In a cave in northern Spain, there is a pile of bones that should not make sense.
63: 
64: The site is called Sima de los Huesos. The Pit of Bones. It sits inside the Atapuerca cave system, and the people in it died around 430,000 years ago. Not modern humans. An older branch of the family, pre-Neanderthal, living through a cold stretch of the Ice Age in Europe.
65: 
66: Here is what is strange. When researchers went through those bones, they found damage that arrives in cycles. Growth that stops and then starts again. Seasonal marks. Signs of a body that was not getting what it needed, over and over, in the same rhythm, year after year.
67: 
68: It looks like the pattern you see in animals that hibernate.
69: 
70: So a study put forward the idea that these people, when the food ran out and the winter got long, might have gone into caves and slowed themselves down. Not full hibernation like a bear. Something closer to a starving sleep, and then they waited for spring.
71: 
72: Other scientists pushed back hard on that. There are plenty of reasons bone growth can stall, and none of them have to involve hibernation. So I am not going to pretend this is settled. It is not.
73: 
74: Here is what is settled. Everything else in this video.
75: 
76: So, the plan. Six jobs. Six jobs the human body cannot do in an Ice Age winter. Stay warm. Cut and build. Wear something. Sleep somewhere. Eat. And stay together, through months of dark, without going insane or getting eaten.
77: 
78: Every one of those jobs needed a fix, and the fixes are some of the best things our species has ever made. By the end, you will know why a hole in a bone matters more than a mammoth, and you will know what those bones in Spain are actually telling us.
79: 
80: [CLIP: Pit of Bones site photograph, bone pile, Atapuerca caption with 430,000 year date]
81: 
82: ## [1:10-2:10] JOB ONE: OWN THE NIGHT
83: 
84: Job one. Stay warm.
85: 
86: Humans have been using fire for an extremely long time. The working estimate is at least 300,000 to 400,000 years of it. By the middle of the last Ice Age, fire was not a bonus. It was the difference between a night and a last night.
87: 
88: And they were far more deliberate about it than you would guess. Archaeologists digging Ice Age fire pits in Ukraine turned up rough little campfires, exactly as expected. Then they found built fireplaces. Constructed on purpose, laid out on purpose, and one of them had burned at over 600 degrees Celsius. That is hotter than 1,100 degrees Fahrenheit. That is not a campfire. That is a kiln.
89: 
90: [CLIP: Ukraine hearth excavation, animated temperature comparison graphic]
91: 
92: When wood ran short out on the open steppe, they burned bone and animal fat instead. Fire cooked their food, hardened wooden tools, and bought them hours of light in a season where the sun barely shows up at all.
93: 
94: Warmth solved, as long as you never leave. Which is a problem, because you have to leave.
95: 
96: ## [2:10-3:15] JOB TWO: BORROW A BETTER BODY
97: 
98: Job two is the one everybody skips, and it is the one every other job depends on. Tools.
99: 
100: Somewhere between 22,000 and 18,000 years ago, in what is now France, Spain and Portugal, people were making flint work that is genuinely hard to believe. We call it Solutrean, and the signature piece is a point shaped like a leaf.
101: 
102: In 1874, near the village of Volgu in France, workers uncovered a cache of these. The best one is around 35 centimeters long. Over a foot of flint, thinned almost flat, with the edges worked so finely that the first archaeologists to see it did not believe it was ancient. Getting that shape out of rock requires pressure flaking, where you push off tiny chips with a pointed tool instead of striking, and it is unforgiving. One bad chip and you start over.
103: 
104: [CLIP: Volgu laurel leaf point, scale bar for the 35cm specimen]
105: 
106: You need a point like that to bring down something large. You need a blade to cut hide. You need a scraper to soften that hide so it stops being a board and starts being clothing. Every single item in the rest of this video begins as a rock that a person shaped on purpose.
107: 
108: ## [3:15-4:45] JOB THREE: WEAR THE ANIMAL
109: 
110: Job three. Wear something.
111: 
112: The first version was the obvious one. Take the hide off an animal that was already built for the cold, and put it on yourself.
113: 
114: You can see it in the bones. In northern Europe, there are bear paw bones from at least 300,000 years ago carrying cut marks in exactly the places you would slice to pull a pelt off clean. Somebody was skinning bears for the fur, not for the meat.
115: 
116: [CLIP: Bear paw bone with cut marks visible, close macro]
117: 
118: But a loose hide draped over your shoulders leaks heat out of every gap. And an Ice Age winter finds every gap. The fix for that is tiny, and it is the most underrated object in this entire story.
119: 
120: The eyed needle. A thin sliver of bone or ivory, with a hole drilled through the end.
121: 
122: The earliest ones we have come from Denisova Cave in Siberia, around 40,000 years ago, and a 2024 paper in Science Advances traced eyed needles spreading across northern Eurasia right around then. A needle means seams. Seams mean fitted sleeves, cuffs that close at the wrist, layers you can move in. There is a real difference between draping an animal over yourself and wearing it. One of those keeps you alive on a long hunt.
123: 
124: [CLIP: Denisova Cave needle artifact, then animated seam vs. drape heat-loss comparison]
125: 
126: And then there is the detail that makes people wince. Before heading out, hunters would smear animal fat, tallow, across their face and neck. It seals the skin, shuts down wind chill, and slows heat loss right where you lose it fastest. Gross. Effective.
127: 
128: ## [4:45-5:15] MIDPOINT RE-HOOK
129: 
130: So take stock. They had fire hot enough to be a kiln. They had cutting tools good enough to be art. They were wearing fitted animal skin with fat smeared on their faces.
131: 
132: That covers you for maybe three days of an Ice Age winter. Not three months.
133: 
134: Because cold was never the real killer. The real killer is that everything I just described only works if you have somewhere to come back to. And an Ice Age hands you a landscape with no caves and almost no trees.
135: 
136: Which brings us to the invention that is the closest thing to a miracle on this list. In central Ukraine, people built houses out of the skeletons of animals that outweighed them ten to one. The bones in one of those structures date to between about 18,250 and 17,750 years ago, which means that spot was in use for over four hundred years.
137: [CLIP: Mezhyrich excavation photograph, bone circle visible in plan view]
138: 
139: Before I show you the rest of that build, I want your guess. They needed a door in a place where the air outside sits at thirty below. What did they do with that doorway, and why? Put your answer in the comments, and then keep watching, because the actual solution is not what you would design.
140:

8: ## [5:15–7:20] JOB FOUR: BUILD SOMEWHERE TO SLEEP
9: 
10: Here's the part of this story that never makes the museum display.
11: 
12: You've seen the photograph. A ring of mammoth bones out on the Ukrainian steppe, arranged like something ritual, and it looks crude. It looks like the last resort of people with no caves and no trees.
13: 
14: Then you find out what the doorway was doing, and "crude" stops being the right word.
15: 
16: The site is Mezhyrich, in central Ukraine. Four dwellings. A 2025 radiocarbon re-dating study concluded the main structure was in use for as long as 429 years. The same spot. Four centuries. Nobody rebuilds a bad idea for four hundred years.
17: 
18: The frame was mammoth jawbones, stacked and interlocked, with tusks arched over the top like ribs. Hides went over that, fat side out. And notice the order there — structure on the inside, insulation on the outside. That's not an accident. That's a decision somebody made and then kept making.
19: 
20: But the entry is the real evidence. These weren't bubbles with a flap over the hole. You went in through a long, low passage. Crawl in, and the wind is already off you. The cold air you dragged in behind you sinks and drains along the floor instead of rolling over the hearth where people are sleeping. Cold air is heavy. They knew that in their hands long before anyone could write it down.
21: 
22: So that's the answer to the guess I asked you for. The doorway wasn't a door. It was a filter.
23: 
24: And then they did the thing that makes me laugh every time. If your house is a dome of bone and hide, snow is not your enemy anymore. Snow is free. You pile it up the outside and you've just added a metre of the best insulator in the entire landscape. Arctic builders were still doing exactly this a few thousand years ago, because the physics never changed.
25: 
26: [CLIP: Mezhyrich site plan with the entrance passage highlighted, then a cold-air-flow animation showing the heavier air pooling in the corridor]
27: 
28: So they're warm, they're dry, they've got a fire burning like a kiln. Which raises the question that ends every comfortable moment in the Ice Age. What exactly are you eating in February?
29: 
30: ## [7:20–8:40] JOB FIVE: HUNT BIG, KEEP EVERYTHING
31: 
32: Job five. Eat.
33: 
34: Getting food in an Ice Age winter is not a hunting problem. It's an arithmetic problem. One reindeer is three days of calories for one family, and you need a hundred and twenty days of winter.
35: 
36: So they stopped hunting one animal at a time. At the Rock of Solutré, in eastern France, the deposits sit against a limestone cliff and record use by four Paleolithic cultures across roughly twenty-five thousand years — horse bone on top of horse bone, in layers. The site was found in 1866 by Adrien Arcelin and Henry Testot-Ferry, and it's still one of the densest concentrations of horse remains in Europe. The working explanation is a drive: push a herd against ground it can't climb, and the landscape does the killing.
37: 
38: [CLIP: Solutré cliff and bone layer stratigraphy]
39: 
40: Then the harder half of the job. Not getting meat. Keeping it.
41: 
42: Freezing, drying, smoking, burying meat in cold ground and sinking it into cold water. And every one of those methods is really the same idea: hold the food at a temperature where bacteria give up. They didn't know bacteria existed. They knew which hole in the ground ruined meat and which one didn't. That's three hundred thousand years of trial and error doing the work of a thermometer.
43: 
44: ## [8:40–9:40] JOB SIX: STAY TOGETHER
45: 
46: Job six is the one that isn't a technology at all, and it might be the most important.
47: 
48: Body heat. Not a metaphor — literally the cheapest fuel source available, and it scales beautifully. One person in a hide is warm. Six people in a hide are a furnace, and the smaller the space, the fewer calories you burn staying alive.
49: 
50: Which means group living wasn't a cultural preference. It was a survival calculation. Get isolated in an Ice Age winter and you're not just lonely. You're burning your own body at the most expensive rate on the menu.
51: 
52: And you can read the priority in who gets fed. When food runs short, the people a group protects first tell you exactly what that group thinks it needs to keep going. That logic is cold. But it kept the line alive.
53: 
54: ## [9:40–10:25] THE DARK TURN
55: 
56: Because here's the thing I'm not going to skip, and plenty of Ice Age documentaries do.
57: 
58: At Gough's Cave in Somerset, England, there are human remains from about 14,700 years ago. A 2015 study found human tooth marks on the bones. Not animal marks — human ones. Three skulls had been carefully worked into cups.
59: 
60: [CLIP: Gough's Cave skull cup, close on modification]
61: 
62: I'm not going to tell you a tidy story about that. Specialists still argue about whether it was ritual, or hunger, or something that was both at once. What I can tell you is what it means for this episode. They spent hundreds of thousands of years building the greatest survival toolkit our species has ever assembled, and a bad enough winter could still beat it. This isn't a story about conquering the Ice Age. It's a story about staying one step ahead of it.
63: 
64: ## [10:25–11:10] THE HUMOR BEAT: THE FURNACE WAS A COW
65: 
66: Okay. Breathe. Because the next part is genuinely ridiculous.
67: 
68: You want to know how long humans used living animals as central heating? Thousands of years after the Ice Age, European farmers were still building houses with the cows on the ground floor and the family upstairs. In parts of Scandinavia and the Alps, this was standard architecture for centuries. The body heat from the herd came up through the floorboards. The house was the animal.
69: 
70: Imagine explaining that to a heating engineer. "So the boiler is downstairs." "Great, gas or oil?" "Holstein."
71: 
72: And the honest part is that it worked. Warm floor, free fuel, and a smell you simply stopped noticing. Which tells you something about comfort — it's whatever your neighbours also have.
73: 
74: ## [11:10–11:55] THE GEAR NOBODY MENTIONS
75: 
76: One more piece of equipment, and I want to be straight about the dates here, because this one is often the wrong way round.
77: 
78: Snow goggles. A curved plate with a narrow slit, worn so your eyes survive a landscape made of reflected sunlight. Inuit and Yupik makers cut them from whalebone, driftwood, walrus ivory, antler — whatever floated or died nearby. The Canadian Museum of History describes examples recovered from an early Inuit house on Baffin Island.
79: 
80: [CLIP: Inuit snow goggles, slit detail]
81: 
82: Here's the honest note. This evidence is much later than the Ice Age, and it's Arctic rather than European. But the problem it solves is ancient: glare off snow can literally blind you, and a blinded hunter on a glacier in February is a dead hunter. The slit version is the fix, and once you've seen it you cannot unsee it.
83: 
84: ## [11:55–12:45] THE BODY ITSELF
85: 
86: And now the plot twist.
87: 
88: Everything up to this point has been a story about inventing our way out of the cold. Tools, houses, needles, goggles. People solving a problem with an object.
89: 
90: Then you meet the Yaghan.
91: 
92: The Yaghan lived in Tierra del Fuego, at the bottom of South America, in freezing wind and near-freezing water. Darwin saw them in the 1830s during the Beagle voyage and was genuinely baffled — people living through that climate with almost nothing on. A 2021 study using bone density and genomic analysis described the Fuegians as an exemplary cold-adapted population. Reviews of circumpolar populations have found elevated resting metabolic rates as a recurring pattern across cold-climate groups.
93: 
94: They didn't beat the cold with a cupboard full of gear. Their bodies ran hotter. The furnace got turned up at the factory, over generations, in the same species you're in.
95: 
96: [CLIP: Tierra del Fuego, wind across the water, then a split-screen comparison of insulation vs. metabolic output]
97: 
98: Which reframes everything before it. The inventions weren't the only strategy. They were the strategy for people whose bodies couldn't change fast enough. The Yaghan are what the other path looks like.
99: 
100: ## [12:45–15:00] PAYOFF AND CLOSE: BACK TO THE PIT
101: 
102: So. Back to Spain. Back to the bones that started this.
103: 
104: In 2020, a study in the journal *L'Anthropologie* proposed that the Sima de los Huesos hominins, around 430,000 years ago, may have survived hard winters in a state like hibernation — a slowed, starving sleep, waiting out the worst of it.
105: 
106: And I told you at the start that I wouldn't pretend it was settled, so here's the honest version. It isn't. Other researchers point out that interrupted bone growth has several mundane explanations — malnutrition, disease, ordinary seasonal stress — and that no human population is known to hibernate. The site itself is a deep shaft where bodies accumulated over time, which complicates what any of those skeletons can tell us about how the people lived.
107: 
108: So the answer is: maybe. Probably not in the way the headline suggests. But possibly in a way we haven't ruled out. That's where real science leaves you, and I'd rather leave you there than hand you a fact that isn't one.
109: 
110: Here's what isn't in doubt.
111: 
112: The body you're sitting in cannot do an Ice Age winter. No fur, no fat layer worth the name, no hibernation, no claws. Everything that kept our ancestors alive through hundreds of thousands of years of cold was something they worked out and then handed down: a shaped rock, a hole drilled through a splinter of bone, a house with a corridor, a cached haunch of meat, six people breathing in a small dark room.
113: 
114: Not one of those is impressive on its own. Together they're the reason there's a person reading this.
115: 
116: So next time you're cold — actually cold, waiting for a bus, and annoyed about it — notice something. You're not scared. That's new. For most of human history, cold was a thing that could kill you by Thursday, and the fact that it's now an inconvenience is a stack of unglamorous inventions and one hole in a piece of bone.
117: 
118: You are what those people built. Which means the least you can do with a winter is use it well.
119: 
120: And if you guessed the doorway thing before I explained it — leave a comment and tell me, because I want to know how common that instinct is.

Gough's Cave cited to "Bello et al., 2015, Journal of Human Evolution." Mezhyrich cited to a 2025 radiocarbon study in Open Research Europe. | **Step B by a mile** — this is research-paper-level sourcing |

Midpoint re-hook includes a direct audience question ("What did they do with the doorway? Put your answer in the comments") | **Step B** — systematically engineered retention |

Cited to a 2015 study.** Then: "This isn't a story about conquering the Ice Age. It's a story about staying one step ahead of it." | **Step B** — specific, brutal, honest, and reframes the whole narrative |
